A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BenchBuilder/Arena-Hard research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons, prompt-quality experiments, judge comparisons, random-subset evaluations, and appendix analyses of verbosity and repeated runs.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds WildChat experiments, alternative-annotator tests, style-control experiments, and self-bias analyses.

M1.justification: Section 6.5 and Appendix A.2 introduce style-controlled scoring: the Bradley-Terry model gains covariates for response length and markdown features, changing how model strengths are estimated. This is a substantive new evaluation component. The underlying seven-quality curation approach and GPT-4/Gemini judge ensemble already appear in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation using WildChat user–ChatGPT conversations, extending beyond Chatbot Arena evaluation traffic. It processes 150,000 queries and constructs the 250-prompt Wild-Hard-Auto benchmark, evaluated against a random WildChat subset. This materially broadens evidence across data sources; the English, single-turn scope remains.

E2.justification: The main MT-Bench/AlpacaEval comparisons and four individual judges plus ensemble are retained. Supplementary comparisons change: v2 Table 12 adds a length-only judging policy, while the GPT-versus-Claude length-bias comparison in v1 Table 7 is replaced by comparisons between uncontrolled and style-controlled GPT-4 judging.

E3.justification: v2 introduces style-controlled human reference rankings, Kendall tau reporting, a 250-prompt WildChat evaluation, and a 10-model alternative-annotator experiment. Section 4.2 also revises the reported filtering recipe and thresholds, without establishing that the original benchmark was regenerated. Both versions retain 500 Arena-Hard prompts and 1,000 judgments; the table's 1,000-to-500 prompt-count correction does not establish a reduced evaluation budget.

E4.justification: v2 tests dependence on the prompt annotator, expands verbosity experiments to three models and markdown manipulations, and adds style-control and model-family self-bias analyses. Conversely, v1's calibration plots, three-run stability table, and second music judgment example disappear. The quality-score sensitivity plots and original Arena random-subset comparison are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 95% confidence intervals from 100 bootstrap rounds. v2 removes v1 Table 8's explicit reporting of three separate GPT-3.5 evaluation runs. Appendix A.1 expands the bootstrap explanation, but does not establish additional repeated evaluations or an increased run count.

E6.justification: In the general English comparison, Arena-Hard confidence agreement changes from 89.1% to 90.9%, while Spearman correlation changes from 94.1% to 93.2% (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1). Hard-prompt agreement changes from 92.0% to 98.6%. v2 adds WildChat, annotator, style-control, and self-bias results and revises the leaderboard. Its headline 98.6% figure comes from different comparison conditions than v1's headline 89.1%.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a formal style-augmented Bradley-Terry objective, covariate definitions, and proportional feature normalization. Appendix A.1 also qualifies the existing Gaussian approximation and describes empirical probability estimation when normality fails. The original three benchmark metrics remain; the substantial mathematical addition concerns style-controlled estimation, not new theorems.

C1.justification: v2 expands the introductory claims to cross-source robustness and mitigation of LLM-judge biases. Its headline changes from 89.1% agreement at $25 to 98.6% correlation/agreement at $20, and from threefold tighter confidence intervals to threefold higher separation. These revise the claimed evaluation capabilities and quantitative guarantees, although the central automated-curation contribution remains.

C2.justification: v1 primarily treats verbosity and self-bias as limitations. v2 interprets new experiments as evidence of separating substance from style, resistance to length/markdown gaming, and reduced self-bias through ensembles. It adds reasons for excluding multilingual and multi-turn evaluation, while removing the calibration caveat accompanying v1 Figure 5. The anti-gaming interpretation is broader than the tested manipulations establish.

D1.justification: v2 documents style features, normalization, and new markdown-manipulation system prompts. It specifies sampling two prompts from each selected cluster and adds annotation-cost estimates of approximately $500 with GPT-4-Turbo or $45 with Llama-3-70B, including token-price assumptions. These substantially extend technical and resource information; the original annotation and judging prompt templates are retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds WildBench, LiveBench, MixEval, BigCodeBench, WildChat, and Chatbot Arena style control. The introduction and new classification figure sharpen the existing positioning around automated, configurable, open-ended curation. The reference to Verga et al.'s ensemble-judge work is removed despite retaining ensemble judging. These are targeted changes within the established research framing.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. Sections 4–6 are reorganized around pipeline costs, generalizability, and bias mitigation; limitations are rewritten; Brier-score background and prompt examples move into dedicated appendices. The benchmark name drops 'v0.1', and references change from numbered to author-year citations.

P2.justification: v2 adds a benchmark-classification figure and multiple robustness and style-control tables, removes the calibration figure and repeated-run table, and substantially expands the leaderboard. Existing plots are rearranged, benchmark-table columns are reordered with a Kendall tau row added, and several main-text tables move to the appendix. These substantially change the presentation beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens two important weaknesses in v1: limited validation beyond the original data/annotator and acknowledged judging biases without a tested style-control remedy. WildChat and alternative-annotator experiments broaden validation, while Sections 6.5 and A.2 provide an implemented, documented mitigation supported by controlled experiments. Removing calibration and repeated-run evidence reduces transparency, and the broad anti-gaming and 98.6% headline claims need qualification. Nevertheless, the added validation and actionable bias treatment provide a substantial net improvement.
